topic.angle: George & Hwang PTH ratio, anchoring bias exploitation

papers.title: Short-term Momentum and Reversals, Turnover, and a Stock's Price-to-52-week-High Ratio
papers.hypothesis: Rank stocks on a composite of PTH ratio and trailing turnover: high-PTH + high-turnover stocks exhibit short-term momentum continuation, while low-PTH + low-turnover stocks exhibit reversals — use PTH×turnover z-score as the ranking signal instead of raw past return.
papers.rationale: Published in Journal of Empirical Finance 2024; results hold in both large- and small-cap subsamples and survive Fama-French 5-factor adjustment. The PTH×turnover interaction is a direct drop-in ranking signal: compute each stock's current price / 52-week-high (PTH) and 21-day average dollar volume z-score, multiply them, rank cross-sectionally. Skipping 5 days avoids the micro-reversal that contaminates formation-end contamination. For a daily rebalancing strategy, this could replace or augment the 12-1 return rank with a more behaviorally grounded signal that is explicitly forward in information content.

papers.title: Dynamic Anchoring, 52-Week High, and Return Predictability
papers.hypothesis: Rank stocks on the 3-month change in PTH ratio (ΔPTH = PTH_now − PTH_63_days_ago) rather than the PTH level: rising PTH signals accelerating anchor-driven underreaction and predicts stronger continuation than static PTH alone.
papers.rationale: Chou, Ko, and Yang (SSRN 4157874) show that static PTH level conflates stocks on different trajectories; the time-varying change in PTH isolates the marginal anchoring pressure and earns incremental alpha over static PTH. Implementation is straightforward: form ΔPTH = (close / rolling_max(close, 252)) over a 63-day difference, rank cross-sectionally at each rebalance. This pairs naturally with an existing 12-1 momentum rank as a confirmation filter or a secondary sort, adding a behaviorally distinct dimension without look-ahead.

papers.title: Momentum Crashes and the 52-Week High
papers.hypothesis: Construct PTH-neutral momentum by double-sorting on 12-1 past return and PTH quintile, then going long high-past-return / high-PTH and short low-past-return / low-PTH stocks to eliminate the speculative PTH-far component that drives momentum crashes.
papers.rationale: Byun and Jeon (published Marquette 2023) document that momentum crashes are concentrated in stocks far from their 52-week high (low PTH) that attract speculative demand during market rebounds; filtering these out substantially reduces left-tail drawdowns while preserving upside. For a walk-forward strategy targeting Sharpe stability, excluding low-PTH winner stocks from the long leg and low-PTH loser stocks from the short leg is a clean regime-robust filter. Negative windows (the primary penalty in the walk-forward objective) should shrink materially.

papers.title: Overnight Returns, Daytime Reversals, and Anchoring Bias
papers.hypothesis: Use PTH < 0.85 as a regime filter: stocks significantly below their 52-week high show a persistent anchoring premium in overnight sessions that accumulates into positive medium-term drift, making PTH-based screening a useful complement to price-return ranking for the long leg.
papers.rationale: Kim and Goh (Applied Economics Letters 2025, SSRN 4482812) isolate anchoring premium as an overnight phenomenon: noise investors anchor to the 52-week high at close, creating a predictable drift that arbitrageurs cannot fully close intraday. For a daily-rebalancing cross-sectional strategy, ranking on cumulative overnight returns (close_{t-1} to open_{t}) over the past 21 days and using PTH as a secondary sort provides a signal orthogonal to 12-1 return. The result is negative for stocks very near their 52-week high (where anchoring upward suppresses further gains), making PTH a non-linear gate rather than a linear rank.

papers.title: Anchoring, the 52-Week High and Post-Earnings Announcement Drift
papers.hypothesis: Amplify earnings-momentum signals by interacting standardized unexpected earnings (SUE) with the stock's PTH: positive-surprise stocks near their 52-week high (high PTH) exhibit the largest PEAD continuation because analysts anchor their revisions to the 52-week high anchor, producing systematic under-revision.
papers.rationale: George, Hwang, and Li (SSRN 2391455) show that PTH and earnings surprises interact multiplicatively: SUE×PTH cross-sectional rank generates alpha well beyond either variable alone because anchored analyst forecasts cause systematic underreaction to earnings beats near the 52-week high. This is directly implementable with daily price data (use TTM EPS estimate proxies or rolling 63-day return surprises as a SUE proxy) and adds a fundamental-behavioral dimension absent from pure price-momentum strategies, potentially helping in periods when price momentum alone stalls.
